metadata.title: Do teachers’ years of experience make a difference in the quality of teaching?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a convenience sample of 80 primary-school teachers from seven government schools in Queensland, Australia, with classroom observations conducted using the CLASS K-3 protocol (Prep to Grade 3). The analysis is based on standard classroom observation scores and teacher-reported years of experience, with grade level taught included as a covariate in ANCOVA models. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures, and the statistical approach is not framed as a population-representative ILSA-style estimation. As a result, the findings should be interpreted as evidence about observed classroom processes in this sampled context rather than as nationally representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not use ILSA-style cognitive achievement outcomes with Plausible Values; instead, it analyzes CLASS observational domain and dimension scores (7-point ratings) and teacher years-of-experience categories. Because the dependent variables are direct observational ratings rather than PV-based achievement scales, PV handling is not applicable. The paper also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure for the analytic dataset, so missing-data handling is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample comprises 80 teachers who participated in both classroom observations and individual interviews, with only the first year of data used for any teacher who participated multiple times to avoid duplicating teacher scores. Teachers were drawn from seven government primary schools in Queensland, Australia, and observations used the CLASS K-3 measure (Prep to Grade 3) with at least four 30-minute observation cycles per classroom (minimum 2 hours total observation time). Teachers were categorized by years of experience into two groups (0–3 years vs. >3 years) and three groups (0–3, 4–5, and >5 years). The manuscript does not report additional exclusions beyond the longitudinal first-year rule.

The dataset consists of CLASS K-3 classroom observation scores (Emotional Support, Classroom Organisation, Instructional Support) from 80 Queensland primary-school teachers teaching Prep to Grade 3, with grade level taught included as a covariate. Across two experience groupings (0–3 vs. >3 years), there were no significant differences in any CLASS domain or dimension. Across three groupings (0–3, 4–5, >5 years), Classroom Organisation differed significantly, with the 4–5 “transitioning” group scoring lower; at the dimension level, Negative Climate, Behaviour Management, and Instructional Learning Formats showed significant differences. The study’s limitation is that it is a small, non-representative convenience sample and does not report missing-data handling; additionally, the CLASS instrument is US-developed and may be culturally bounded. data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse for ML-specific fields because the article does not train or evaluate any machine learning models and does not use ILSA/PV-based achievement outcomes. The study is an observational classroom-quality analysis using CLASS ratings and ANCOVA, so plausible values, PV handling, and ML technique lists are not applicable. Consequently, main_findings is left empty because the schema requires StructuredFinding rows only for empirical ML/predictive papers, which this paper is not.
